claims.text: The target alloy has titanium and nickel as primary constituents, with possible additional Cr, Co, and Fe.
Each alloy component is constrained to 5–35 at%.
The conventionally processed initial microstructure has predominantly straight grain boundaries.
Reducing the cooling rate after solution heat treatment permits coarsening of L12-structured gamma-prime precipitates.
Coarsened precipitates interfere with mobile grain boundaries and produce a serrated grain-boundary morphology.
Heat-treatment durations of approximately 1–100 hours can provide sufficient precipitate coarsening.
A cooling-rate window exists that enables precipitate coarsening while preventing precipitate overgrowth or microstructural degradation.
Serrated grain boundaries distribute local strains more evenly than straight grain boundaries.
More even strain distribution reduces stress concentration along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary serration mitigates intergranular cracking and elevated-temperature hot-ductility loss.
Reduced-rate cooling and the resulting grain-boundary serration increase tensile fracture strain at approximately 650°C relative to rapid cooling.
Reduced-rate cooling and the resulting grain-boundary serration increase creep rupture life at approximately 650°C relative to rapid cooling.
Conventional rapid cooling yields straight grain boundaries and typical high-temperature ductility drops.
The intervention is effective over an operating range near 600–700°C.
Conditions outside the proposed processing boundaries may cause either insufficient grain-boundary modification or deleterious microstructural overgrowth.
The quantitative improvement depends on cooling rate, composition, and heat-treatment duration.
Failure to obtain at least a 10% increase in tensile fracture strain or creep rupture life relative to the rapid-cooled control is designated as a falsifying result.
Failure to observe serrated grain boundaries after reduced-rate cooling is designated as a falsifying result.
